Criterion A: Analysing:
# Criterion A: Analysing
## What it assesses
Criterion A: Analysing assesses how well you analyse texts. The strands ask you to analyse the content, context, language, structure, technique and style of texts and how they create meaning; analyse the effects of the creator's choices on an audience; justify opinions and ideas using examples, explanations and terminology; and evaluate similarities and differences by connecting features across and within texts.

## How to do well
Use the PEEL structure: make a point, give evidence, explain its effect and link back to the question. Name techniques precisely, such as metaphor, juxtaposition and foreshadowing. Explain why the writer made a choice and its effect on the reader.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Analysis: examining how parts of a text create meaning
PEEL: point, evidence, explanation, link
Technique: a method a writer uses to create an effect
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion B: Organizing:
# Criterion B: Organizing
## What it assesses
Criterion B: Organizing assesses how well you structure your work. The strands ask you to employ organizational structures that serve the context and intention; organize opinions and ideas in a sustained, coherent and logical manner; and use referencing and formatting tools to create a presentation style suitable to the context and intention.

## How to do well
Plan before writing. Use a clear introduction with a thesis, paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion. Use transitions such as furthermore, however and consequently. Reference quotations and sources consistently.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Thesis: the main argument of a piece of writing
Topic sentence: a sentence stating the point of a paragraph
Coherence: ideas connected logically and clearly
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion C: Producing text:
# Criterion C: Producing text
## What it assesses
Criterion C: Producing text assesses your own creative and analytical writing and speaking. The strands ask you to produce texts that demonstrate insight, imagination and sensitivity while exploring and reflecting critically on new perspectives and ideas; make stylistic choices in terms of linguistic, literary and visual devices, demonstrating awareness of impact on an audience; and select relevant details and examples to develop ideas.

## How to do well
Choose a form, voice and register that suit your purpose and audience. Make deliberate stylistic choices and be ready to explain them in a rationale. Develop ideas with specific detail.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Stylistic choice: a deliberate decision about language or form
Voice: the distinctive personality of a piece of writing
Rationale: an explanation of the choices you made
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion D: Using language:
# Criterion D: Using language
## What it assesses
Criterion D: Using language assesses accuracy and range of language. The strands ask you to use appropriate and varied vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; write and speak in a register and style that serve the context and intention; use correct grammar, syntax and punctuation; spell (alphabetic languages) or write (character languages) with accuracy; and use appropriate non-verbal communication techniques.

## How to do well
Vary sentence length and structure. Choose precise vocabulary. Proofread for punctuation, agreement and spelling. Match formality to the audience.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Register: the level of formality of language
Syntax: the arrangement of words in sentences
Vocabulary: the range of words used
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required

# Communication
## The key concept
Communication is the exchange or transfer of signals, facts, ideas and symbols. It requires a sender, a message and an intended receiver, and involves a shared code. It is one of the sixteen MYP key concepts, broad ideas that connect subjects. A key concept is a big idea that frames a unit of inquiry, and each unit also uses related concepts specific to the subject.

## In Language and Literature
Writers communicate ideas through form, language and structure; readers decode them. Related concepts include audience imperatives, purpose and style.

Related concept: a concept specific to one subject

Reading and analysing fiction:
# Reading and analysing fiction
## Elements of fiction
Fiction is imaginative prose such as novels and short stories. Plot is the sequence of events; it often follows exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Characterization is how a writer creates characters, through description, dialogue and actions. Setting is the time and place of a story. Narrative perspective is who tells the story: first person, third person limited or omniscient. Theme is a central idea a text explores.

## Analysing
Look at how the writer uses imagery, symbolism, foreshadowing and dialogue. Ask why the writer made each choice and what effect it has on the reader.

## Key terms
Plot: the sequence of events in a story
Characterization: how a writer creates characters
Setting: the time and place of a story
Narrative perspective: who tells the story
Theme: a central idea a text explores
Foreshadowing: hints of what will happen later
Poetry:
# Poetry
## Poetic devices
Poetry uses concentrated language, sound and form. A stanza is a group of lines. Rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhymes; meter is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Imagery appeals to the senses. A metaphor states one thing is another; a simile compares using like or as. Personification gives human qualities to non-human things. Alliteration repeats initial sounds; enjambment runs a sentence over a line break.

## Forms
Forms include the sonnet (14 lines), haiku, free verse, ballad and ode. Analyse how form and sound reinforce meaning.

## Key terms
Stanza: a group of lines in a poem
Metaphor: saying one thing is another
Simile: a comparison using like or as
Enjambment: a sentence running over a line break
Free verse: poetry without regular rhyme or meter
Sonnet: a 14-line poem
Drama:
# Drama
## Elements of drama
Drama is written to be performed. A script contains dialogue and stage directions. A monologue is a long speech by one character; a soliloquy is a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts alone on stage. Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not.

## Analysing drama
Consider how staging, lighting, sound, costume and movement create meaning. Tragedy shows the downfall of a protagonist, often through a flaw; comedy usually ends happily. Conflict drives the action.

## Key terms
Stage directions: instructions in a script about action and staging
Soliloquy: a character speaking thoughts alone on stage
Dramatic irony: the audience knowing what a character does not
Tragedy: a play showing the downfall of a protagonist
Protagonist: the main character
Non-fiction and media texts:
# Non-fiction and media texts
## Types of text
Non-fiction texts include articles, speeches, letters, biographies and essays. Media texts include advertisements, films, podcasts, websites and social media posts. Every text has a purpose, such as to inform, persuade, entertain or instruct, and a target audience.

## Analysing
Persuasive techniques include rhetorical questions, emotive language, statistics, repetition and the rule of three. Ethos appeals to credibility, pathos to emotion and logos to logic. In visual texts, analyse layout, colour, images and typography. Bias is a one-sided presentation.

## Key terms
Purpose: what a text aims to do
Target audience: the people a text is aimed at
Rhetorical question: a question asked for effect
Emotive language: words chosen to provoke feelings
Bias: a one-sided presentation
Writing for purpose and audience:
# Writing for purpose and audience
## Planning
Before writing, decide the purpose, audience, form and register. Purpose is what you want the writing to do. Audience is who will read it. Form is the type of text, such as a letter, article or story. Register is the level of formality.

## Techniques
Narrative writing uses description, dialogue and structure to tell a story. Persuasive writing uses a clear position, evidence and rhetorical devices. Informative writing uses clear organization, headings and facts. Descriptive writing uses sensory detail and figurative language. Redraft and proofread to improve your work.

## Key terms
Form: the type of text
Persuasive writing: writing that aims to convince
Descriptive writing: writing that creates a picture with detail
Redrafting: revising writing to improve it
Figurative language: language that is not literal, such as metaphor
